node.label: Anna Clark
node.date_label: Women’s Silence, Men’s Violence (1987) · The Struggle for the Breeches (1995) · Scandal (2004) · Desire (2008; second edition 2019) · Alternative Histories of the Self (2017)
node.description: In The Struggle for the Breeches (1995), Anna Clark argues that British working-class formation depended on conflicts over gender, household authority and work as well as struggles between classes. Radical domestic rhetoric could promise protection and political inclusion while ultimately narrowing the movement around male breadwinners. Carole Turbin praised its integration of gender and class but criticized its repetitive structure and insufficiently explicit links between arguments. Clark’s 1992 study of Chartist domesticity explicitly draws on Gareth Stedman Jones while qualifying Joan Scott’s account of masculine citizenship. Scandal (2004) treats sexual controversy as a force in constitutional politics; William Kuhn praised its explanatory power but objected that Clark sometimes judged historical actors by modern standards. Desire (2008; revised second edition 2019) surveys European sexuality. Alternative Histories of the Self (2017), as Charles Upchurch reads it, shifts attention from finding modern sexual identities to historically specific constructions of self; her 2023 Anne Lister chapter develops queer reading as a method for connecting anatomical texts with readers’ embodied understanding.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Women’s Silence, Men’s Violence: Sexual Assault in England, 1770–1845 (1987); “The Rhetoric of Chartist Domesticity” (1992); The Struggle for the Breeches: Gender and the Making of the British Working Class (1995; paperback 1997); Scandal: The Sexual Politics of the British Constitution (2004); Desire: A History of European Sexuality (2008; revised and expanded second edition 2019); Alternative Histories of the Self: A Cultural History of Sexuality and Secrets, 1762–1917 (2017); “Anne Lister’s Search for the Anatomy of Sex” (2023).
node.scope_note: Selected primary reading: the 1992 Chartism article pp. 62–65 and 87–88; the complete 1998 Vickery review; the 2023 Lister chapter pp. 49–51, 62–65 and 68–70. Turbin and Kuhn reviews read in full; Upchurch’s substantive review read in indexed publisher text after a failed direct fetch. Monographs, original diaries, the Scott, Thompson, Stedman Jones, Davidoff/Hall and Laqueur originals, and Twilight Moments remain unread here; book arguments are bounded by publisher descriptions and named readers.

proposed_edges.relationship: As Carole Turbin explains, The Struggle for the Breeches (1995) draws on E. P. Thompson’s The Making of the English Working Class (1963) in combining culture with institutions and tracing plebeian class formation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Turbin, review PDF p. 1, opening paragraph: “owes much to Thompson”; she specifies culture/institutions and plebeian traditions. This is a named scholarly reader’s attribution. Neither book freshly read; no supervisory or personal relationship inferred.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Rhetoric of Chartist Domesticity” (1992), Clark explicitly follows Stedman Jones’s Languages of Class (1983) in treating Chartist rhetoric as political action rather than simply a reflection of economic distress.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Clark, printed p. 63, opening paragraph and n. 6: “In this I am following”; the note identifies Languages of Class, pp. 90–95. Selected primary passage read. The essay’s earlier 1982 publication and the 1983 collection are distinct; this claim dates the collection she cites. Original Stedman Jones text unread; selective uptake, not blanket agreement.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Rhetoric of Chartist Domesticity” (1992), Clark qualifies Joan Scott’s account of masculine citizenship by arguing that domestic rhetoric could initially bring women into Chartism, even though its later effects narrowed women’s political scope.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Clark, printed p. 65, paragraph beginning Surprisingly enough, and n. 14; conclusion pp. 87–88. She names Scott alongside Deborah Valenze and counters a fixed opposition between citizenship and community with a “larger notion of politics”. Scott is cited through Gender and the Politics of History (1988), p. 53. Specific qualification of this account; no rejection of Scott’s whole project. Scott’s chapter and the Smith/Valenze article unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Clark’s 1998 review of The Gentleman’s Daughter uses Leonore Davidoff and Catherine Hall’s jointly authored Family Fortunes (1987) to defend historically changing public/private boundaries and domesticity’s role in middle-class formation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Clark review, paragraphs beginning Vickery’s chief target, They demonstrate, This ideology, and Similarly (web-reader lines 55–58). The argument belongs jointly to Davidoff and Hall. Full review read; Family Fortunes itself unread. A resource used in this review, without claiming sole derivation or assigning a jointly authored passage to one author.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Anne Lister’s Search for the Anatomy of Sex” (2023), Clark takes the chronology discussed in Laqueur’s Making Sex (1990) as one starting point, then asks how an individual reader understood anatomical texts.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Clark, printed pp. 49–50 and 63 n. 3, with conclusion p. 63. Opening discusses Laqueur, other historians’ objections, and a gap in work on the early nineteenth century; p. 50 shifts from what experts wrote to women’s interpretations. This is a bounded problem-setting resource, not endorsement of the one-sex/two-sex thesis. Her note cites the 1992 edition; original 1990 retained from the existing Laqueur node. Laqueur’s book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Struggle for the Breeches (1995) makes conflict over work, marriage and domestic authority part of the explanation of British class formation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh reading of the UC Press About the Book description and contents; original 1995 confirmed by Minnesota bibliography, rather than the displayed 1997 paperback. This is publisher-mediated characterization, corroborated by Turbin’s review; full book unread. Projects a named individual contribution from existing group-level routes without replacing them.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Struggle for the Breeches (1995) contrasts artisans and textile workers in Lancashire, Glasgow and London, showing how each created distinctively gendered communities and political strategies.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: UC Press About the Book, regional/occupational comparison and concluding domesticity argument. Publisher description read; full chapters and underlying evidence unread. Existing gender → labourhistory edge_741 names Clark collectively; this new person route preserves that group claim.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Rhetoric of Chartist Domesticity” (1992), Clark treats rhetoric as a set of persuasive strategies that linked political language with domestic experience and could produce contradictory outcomes.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary printed pp. 63–65, especially discussion of persuasion and different tactics, read with conclusion pp. 87–88. The claim concerns her contribution to the debate, not membership of a homogeneous school. Existing edge_1174 names Clark within the debate → gender route; this distinct person endpoint is new.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Anne Lister’s Search for the Anatomy of Sex” (2023), Clark develops queer reading as a way to explain how readers could use hostile texts to understand their desires and bodies.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary printed p. 50, paragraph beginning Because these texts, and conclusion p. 63; n. 9 on p. 64 points back to Alternative Histories of the Self (2017). Selected chapter passages read; original diaries and 2017 book unread. Concerns an interpretive method, not a claim that historical subjects shared modern identity categories.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Masculinities in an Industrializing Society: Britain, 1800–1914 (2005), John Tosh questions the explanation, attributed to Anna Clark’s The Struggle for the Breeches (1995), that shared manhood could bridge class divisions, arguing that its effectiveness required a working-class acceptance of polarized gender identities for which evidence was limited.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher PDF read. Note 39 identifies Clark, p. 2; the body grants partial support before challenging working-class diffusion, citing dual-income households and popular representations of female sexuality. This is a qualified criticism of one explanation.
proposed_edges.map_label: Questions manhood as a bridge across class

proposed_edges.relationship: In Presidential Address: The 1890s Debate over the Democratic Control of Hospitals in Britain and New Zealand (2021), Anna Clark contributes to medical and health history by comparing hospital scandals and interpreting unsuccessful demands for democratic control, patients’ rights and nurses’ health as possible precursors of patient-centered care.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher abstract read, not the article body. It distinguishes these campaigns from economy-driven reform and state-efficiency proposals and cautiously suggests a connection with patient-centered care. The edge records this specific historical intervention, without claiming a demonstrated influence on later medical practice. The journal article appeared in 2021; the abstract identifies an earlier conference plenary in 2018.
